title: CTS Administration & Leadership — Unit 2: The Pastor as Undershepherd & Steward

blocks.en: 📖 Administration & Leadership — Unit 2: The Pastor as Undershepherd & Steward
blocks.es_reference: 📖 Administración y Liderazgo — Unidad 2: El pastor como pastor subordinado y mayordomo

blocks.en: Professor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers
blocks.es_reference: Profesor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers

blocks.en: "Shepherd the flock of God which is among you... not as being lords over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock." — 1 Peter 5:2-3 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Apacentad la grey de Dios que está entre vosotros... no como teniendo señorío sobre los que están a vuestro cuidado, sino siendo ejemplos de la grey." — 1 Pedro 5:2-3 (RVG)

blocks.en: Introduction — The Shepherd on the Hillside
blocks.es_reference: Introducción — El pastor en la ladera

blocks.en: Picture a shepherd on a rocky hillside at dusk. The sheep are scattered — some drifting toward a cliff, some tangled in thorns, a few too weak to keep up. He does not stand at a distance and shout instructions. He walks in among them. He knows their voices and they know his. He carries the weak ones. And he himself is not the owner of the flock; he works for the One who owns it, and one day that Owner will return and ask, "How have you cared for what is Mine?" That picture is not poetry. It is the plain job description of every pastor and every leader in the church of God. In Unit 1 we saw that leadership is a calling carried out in humility. Now we go deeper into what the leader actually is: an undershepherd and a steward, two words that, once you understand them, will govern the rest of your ministry.
blocks.es_reference: Imagine a un pastor en una ladera rocosa al atardecer. Las ovejas están dispersas — algunas se acercan a un despeñadero, otras enredadas en espinos, unas pocas demasiado débiles para seguir el paso. Él no se queda a lo lejos gritando instrucciones. Camina entre ellas. Conoce sus voces y ellas conocen la suya. Carga a las débiles. Y él mismo no es el dueño del rebaño; trabaja para Aquel que lo posee, y un día ese Dueño volverá y preguntará: "¿Cómo has cuidado lo que es Mío?" Esa imagen no es poesía. Es la sencilla descripción del oficio de todo pastor y de todo líder en la iglesia de Dios. En la Unidad 1 vimos que el liderazgo es un llamado llevado a cabo con humildad. Ahora profundizamos en lo que el líder realmente es: un pastor subordinado y un mayordomo, dos palabras que, una vez entendidas, gobernarán el resto de su ministerio.

blocks.en: Not the Owner — The Word "Under"
blocks.es_reference: No el dueño — la palabra "subordinado"

blocks.en: Everything turns on one small syllable: under. Peter, an apostle who could have pulled rank, instead writes to the elders as a fellow elder, and tells them: "Shepherd the flock of God which is among you, serving as overseers" (1 Peter 5:1-2). Note the phrase — the flock of God. Not the flock of the pastor, not the flock of the elders, not the flock of the denomination. The sheep were bought with the blood of Christ, and they belong to Christ, who is the Chief Shepherd. The pastor is an undershepherd: a real shepherd with real authority and real responsibility, but always a second shepherd serving under the first. The moment a leader forgets that small word and begins to think of the church as his — his people, his pulpit, his ministry, his kingdom — he has stopped being a shepherd and started being a thief, however slowly and respectably the theft proceeds.
blocks.es_reference: Todo gira en torno a una idea pequeña: estar bajo otro. Pedro, un apóstol que pudo haber impuesto su rango, escribe en cambio a los ancianos como anciano igual que ellos, y les dice: "Apacentad la grey de Dios que está entre vosotros, cuidando de ella" (1 Pedro 5:1-2). Note la frase — la grey de Dios. No la grey del pastor, ni de los ancianos, ni de la denominación. Las ovejas fueron compradas con la sangre de Cristo, y pertenecen a Cristo, que es el Príncipe de los pastores. El pastor es un pastor subordinado: un pastor verdadero con autoridad y responsabilidad reales, pero siempre un segundo pastor que sirve bajo el primero. En el momento en que un líder olvida esa relación y comienza a pensar en la iglesia como suya — su gente, su púlpito, su ministerio, su reino — ha dejado de ser pastor y ha comenzado a ser ladrón, por lento y respetable que sea el robo.

blocks.en: "Shepherd the flock of God which is among you, serving as overseers, not by compulsion but willingly, not for dishonest gain but eagerly." — 1 Peter 5:2 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Apacentad la grey de Dios que está entre vosotros, cuidando de ella, no por fuerza, sino voluntariamente; no por ganancia deshonesta, sino con ánimo pronto." — 1 Pedro 5:2 (RVG)

blocks.en: The Shepherd's Three Tasks
blocks.es_reference: Las tres tareas del pastor

blocks.en: What does a shepherd actually do? Strip the work down and three tasks remain, and a leader who neglects any one of them is only playing at the office. First, he feeds. The sheep cannot feed themselves; they must be led to green pasture, and for the church that pasture is the Word of God, taught plainly enough that ordinary believers can eat and grow. Second, he leads. Sheep left to themselves scatter and wander into danger, so the shepherd goes ahead of them and they follow his voice; he does not drive them from behind like cattle. Third, he protects. Wolves come — false teaching, division, the slow predators of discouragement and sin — and the shepherd stands between the flock and the danger, even at cost to himself. Feed, lead, protect. The leader who only feeds becomes a lecturer; the one who only leads becomes a driver; the one who only protects becomes a guard at an empty gate. The shepherd does all three because the sheep need all three.
blocks.es_reference: ¿Qué hace en realidad un pastor? Reduzca la obra a lo esencial y quedan tres tareas, y el líder que descuida cualquiera de ellas solo juega al oficio. Primero, alimenta. Las ovejas no pueden alimentarse solas; hay que llevarlas a pastos verdes, y para la iglesia ese pasto es la Palabra de Dios, enseñada con suficiente claridad para que los creyentes comunes coman y crezcan. Segundo, guía. Las ovejas dejadas a sí mismas se dispersan y se meten en peligro, así que el pastor va delante de ellas y ellas siguen su voz; no las arrea por detrás como al ganado. Tercero, protege. Vienen lobos — la falsa enseñanza, la división, los depredadores lentos del desaliento y el pecado — y el pastor se interpone entre el rebaño y el peligro, aun a costa de sí mismo. Alimentar, guiar, proteger. El líder que solo alimenta se vuelve conferencista; el que solo guía se vuelve arriero; el que solo protege se vuelve guardia de una puerta vacía. El pastor hace las tres cosas porque las ovejas necesitan las tres.

blocks.en: The Heart of the Shepherd: How, Not Just What
blocks.es_reference: El corazón del pastor: el cómo, no solo el qué

blocks.en: Peter is not finished with what the shepherd does; he presses into how he does it, and here the passage searches the heart. The shepherd is to serve "not by compulsion but willingly, not for dishonest gain but eagerly; nor as being lords over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock" (1 Peter 5:2-3). Read those three contrasts slowly, for they expose the three diseases of the shepherd's heart. Not by compulsion, but willingly — the man who shepherds only because he is trapped, who would quit tomorrow if he could, has the wrong heart; God loves a willing shepherd. Not for dishonest gain, but eagerly — the man who shepherds for what he can get out of it, money or comfort or status, has made the flock a means to his own ends. Not lording it over them, but being an example — the man who drives the sheep with the heavy hand of a tyrant has forgotten that Christ leads by going first. The true shepherd does not say "Do as I command from a distance"; he says "Follow me as I follow Christ," and he leads from the front, where the danger is.
blocks.es_reference: Pedro no termina con lo que hace el pastor; insiste en el cómo, y aquí el pasaje escudriña el corazón. El pastor ha de servir "no por fuerza, sino voluntariamente; no por ganancia deshonesta, sino con ánimo pronto; no como teniendo señorío sobre los que están a vuestro cuidado, sino siendo ejemplos de la grey" (1 Pedro 5:2-3). Lea esos tres contrastes despacio, porque exponen las tres enfermedades del corazón del pastor. No por fuerza, sino voluntariamente — el hombre que pastorea solo porque está atrapado, que renunciaría mañana si pudiera, tiene el corazón equivocado; Dios ama al pastor dispuesto. No por ganancia deshonesta, sino con ánimo pronto — el hombre que pastorea por lo que puede sacar, dinero o comodidad o posición, ha hecho del rebaño un medio para sus propios fines. No con señorío, sino siendo ejemplo — el hombre que arrea a las ovejas con la mano dura de un tirano ha olvidado que Cristo guía yendo primero. El verdadero pastor no dice "Haced lo que mando desde lejos"; dice "Seguidme como yo sigo a Cristo", y guía desde el frente, donde está el peligro.

blocks.en: The finest pastor I ever knew, I met in a prison. Arthur was converted while serving time in a maximum-security penitentiary, and there, behind the walls, he earned a bachelor's degree from a seminary. When he finished, he came to the prison where I served, as an inmate chaplain. We had started a master's program, and Arthur was among the first to enroll; when he earned his master's in theology, he himself carried most of the teaching of theology for our junior-college classes. But it was not his degrees that set him apart. Of all the dormitories, he asked to live in the one that housed the youngest men just entering prison, so that he could reach them. He walked the cell blocks, and more than once he preached a full sermon to a single inmate locked behind one door. He served in the program that cared for the dying, and would sit up the whole night cleaning a man, tending him, talking softly to him as he passed — and then come to work the next morning. Inmates could buy a few snacks for their lockers; Arthur left his standing open on purpose, so that any man who had nothing could take what he needed. When I stood up at his parole hearing, I told them the simple truth: he was the greatest pastor I had ever met. No one appointed Arthur a leader. He became one the way the Lord said shepherds are made — not by lording over the flock, but by becoming an example to it. People will obey a man who drives them only as far as they must; they will follow a man who serves them to the ends of the earth.
blocks.es_reference: Al mejor pastor que jamás he conocido lo conocí en una prisión. Arthur se convirtió mientras cumplía condena en una penitenciaría de máxima seguridad, y allí, tras los muros, obtuvo una licenciatura de un seminario. Cuando terminó, llegó como capellán interno a la prisión donde yo servía. Habíamos iniciado un programa de maestría, y Arthur fue de los primeros en inscribirse; cuando obtuvo su maestría en teología, él mismo se encargó de gran parte de la enseñanza de teología en nuestras clases de colegio universitario. Pero no fueron sus títulos lo que lo distinguió. De todos los dormitorios, pidió vivir en el que alojaba a los más jóvenes que recién entraban a la prisión, para poder alcanzarlos. Recorría los bloques de celdas, y más de una vez predicó un sermón completo a un solo recluso encerrado tras una puerta. Sirvió en el programa que cuidaba a los moribundos, y pasaba la noche entera limpiando a un hombre, cuidándolo, hablándole en voz baja mientras partía; y a la mañana siguiente se presentaba a trabajar. Los reclusos podían comprar algunos víveres para sus casilleros; Arthur dejaba el suyo abierto a propósito, para que cualquier hombre que no tuviera nada pudiera tomar lo que necesitara. Cuando me puse de pie en su audiencia de libertad condicional, les dije la sencilla verdad: era el mejor pastor que jamás había conocido. Nadie nombró líder a Arthur. Llegó a serlo de la manera en que el Señor dijo que se forman los pastores: no enseñoreándose del rebaño, sino haciéndose ejemplo de él. La gente obedecerá solo hasta donde deba a un hombre que la arrea; seguirá hasta el fin del mundo a un hombre que la sirve.

blocks.en: The Steward Who Must Give Account
blocks.es_reference: El mayordomo que debe dar cuenta

blocks.en: Now set beside the shepherd a second picture: the steward. A steward in the ancient world managed a great house that was not his own; he held the keys, ran the affairs, and commanded the servants, but everything he touched belonged to his master, and the day was coming when the master would call him in to settle accounts. This is why the writer of Hebrews lays so heavy a charge on the leaders of the church: "Obey those who rule over you, and be submissive, for they watch for your souls, as those who must give account" (Hebrews 13:17). Read what the leaders are watching: not the budget first, not the building first, but souls. And read why they watch so carefully: because they must give account for those souls to God Himself. This is the truth that turns administration from a worldly chore into a sacred trust. Every roster, every meeting, every hard conversation is the managing of a house that belongs to Another, and the Master is coming home. The steward who remembers the account he must give handles the smallest matter with care, because he knows that nothing in the Lord's house is too small to answer for.
blocks.es_reference: Ahora ponga junto al pastor una segunda imagen: el mayordomo. Un mayordomo en el mundo antiguo administraba una gran casa que no era suya; tenía las llaves, manejaba los asuntos y mandaba a los siervos, pero todo lo que tocaba pertenecía a su señor, y llegaba el día en que el señor lo llamaría a rendir cuentas. Por eso el escritor de Hebreos pone una carga tan pesada sobre los líderes de la iglesia: "Obedeced a vuestros pastores, y sujetaos a ellos; porque ellos velan por vuestras almas, como quienes han de dar cuenta" (Hebreos 13:17). Lea lo que los líderes vigilan: no el presupuesto primero, no el edificio primero, sino las almas. Y lea por qué vigilan con tanto cuidado: porque han de dar cuenta de esas almas a Dios mismo. Esta es la verdad que convierte la administración de una tarea mundana en una confianza sagrada. Cada lista, cada reunión, cada conversación difícil es la administración de una casa que pertenece a Otro, y el Señor vuelve a casa. El mayordomo que recuerda la cuenta que debe dar maneja el asunto más pequeño con cuidado, porque sabe que nada en la casa del Señor es demasiado pequeño como para no responder por ello.

blocks.en: The Lord Jesus drew this very picture and pressed it home. He asked, "Who then is that faithful and wise steward, whom his master will make ruler over his household, to give them their portion of food in due season?" (Luke 12:42), and He pronounced a blessing on the servant whom the master, when he comes, will find faithfully doing his work. Two things stand out for the church leader. The steward's duty is to give the household their food in due season — the very work of feeding the flock we saw above, now framed as the account a manager must render. And the steward is called faithful and wise: faithful, because the trust is not his own and he must be trustworthy with what belongs to Another; wise, because he must manage with skill and not merely good intentions. The leader who holds both — faithfulness to the Owner and wisdom in the work — is the steward the Master is looking for, and the one He will be glad to find at his post when He returns.
blocks.es_reference: El Señor Jesús pintó esta misma imagen y la grabó en el corazón. Preguntó: "¿Quién es el mayordomo fiel y prudente, al cual su señor pondrá sobre su casa, para que a tiempo les dé su ración?" (Lucas 12:42), y pronunció una bendición sobre el siervo a quien el señor, cuando venga, halle haciendo fielmente su obra. Dos cosas resaltan para el líder de la iglesia. El deber del mayordomo es dar a la casa su ración a tiempo — la misma obra de alimentar a la grey que vimos arriba, ahora enmarcada como la cuenta que un administrador debe rendir. Y al mayordomo se le llama fiel y prudente: fiel, porque la confianza no es suya y debe ser digno de ella con lo que pertenece a Otro; prudente, porque debe administrar con destreza y no solo con buenas intenciones. El líder que tiene ambas — fidelidad al Dueño y prudencia en la obra — es el mayordomo que el Señor busca, y al que se alegrará de hallar en su puesto cuando vuelva.

blocks.en: "Who then is that faithful and wise steward, whom his master will make ruler over his household, to give them their portion of food in due season?" — Luke 12:42 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "¿Quién es el mayordomo fiel y prudente, al cual su señor pondrá sobre su casa, para que a tiempo les dé su ración?" — Lucas 12:42 (RVG)

blocks.en: "Obey those who rule over you, and be submissive, for they watch for your souls, as those who must give account." — Hebrews 13:17 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Obedeced a vuestros pastores, y sujetaos a ellos; porque ellos velan por vuestras almas, como quienes han de dar cuenta." — Hebreos 13:17 (RVG)

blocks.en: The Promise That Sustains
blocks.es_reference: La promesa que sostiene

blocks.en: If the account were the whole story, the work would crush a man. But Peter does not end with the weight; he ends with the reward. "And when the Chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the crown of glory that does not fade away" (1 Peter 5:4). Here is the strength of the undershepherd: he serves a Chief Shepherd who is not a hard, absent master but the One who laid down His own life for the sheep, and who is coming back not only to settle accounts but to reward His faithful servants with a crown that will never wither. The earthly crowns men chase — the larger church, the bigger name, the applause of the crowd — all of them fade, and most of them fade within the man's own lifetime. The crown the Chief Shepherd gives never fades at all. So the undershepherd can pour himself out without bitterness and lead without grasping, because his reward is not in the flock's praise but in the Master's "Well done." Shepherd the flock of God, brother. It is His, not yours. Watch for souls as one who must give account. And serve in the joy of the coming Chief Shepherd, who repays His shepherds with a crown that lasts forever.
blocks.es_reference: Si la cuenta fuera toda la historia, la obra aplastaría a un hombre. Pero Pedro no termina con el peso; termina con la recompensa. "Y cuando aparezca el Príncipe de los pastores, vosotros recibiréis la corona incorruptible de gloria" (1 Pedro 5:4). Aquí está la fuerza del pastor subordinado: sirve a un Príncipe de los pastores que no es un amo duro y ausente, sino Aquel que dio su propia vida por las ovejas, y que vuelve no solo a pedir cuentas sino a recompensar a sus siervos fieles con una corona que nunca se marchitará. Las coronas terrenales que los hombres persiguen — la iglesia más grande, el nombre mayor, el aplauso de la multitud — todas se marchitan, y la mayoría se marchitan dentro de la propia vida del hombre. La corona que da el Príncipe de los pastores no se marchita jamás. Así que el pastor subordinado puede entregarse sin amargura y guiar sin aferrarse, porque su recompensa no está en la alabanza del rebaño sino en el "Bien hecho" del Señor. Apaciente la grey de Dios, hermano. Es de Él, no suya. Vele por las almas como quien ha de dar cuenta. Y sirva en el gozo del Príncipe de los pastores que viene, que recompensa a sus pastores con una corona que dura para siempre.

blocks.en: "And when the Chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the crown of glory that does not fade away." — 1 Peter 5:4 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Y cuando aparezca el Príncipe de los pastores, vosotros recibiréis la corona incorruptible de gloria." — 1 Pedro 5:4 (RVG)

mc.stem: In 1 Peter 5, whose flock is the pastor told to shepherd?
mc.why: Peter calls it 'the flock of God' — the sheep belong to Christ, the Chief Shepherd, not to the pastor.

mc.stem: The word 'undershepherd' chiefly emphasizes that the pastor is:
options: A second shepherd serving under the Chief Shepherd
mc.why: 'Under' means he is a real shepherd but always serves beneath Christ, the first and Chief Shepherd.

mc.stem: Which three tasks summarize the shepherd's work in this unit?
mc.why: The shepherd feeds the flock on the Word, leads from the front, and protects them from wolves.

mc.stem: A leader who only teaches but never leads or protects becomes:
mc.why: Feeding alone, without leading and protecting, reduces the shepherd to a lecturer.

mc.stem: 'Not by compulsion but willingly' addresses the shepherd's:
mc.why: Peter searches the motive: God wants a willing shepherd, not one who serves only because he feels trapped.

mc.stem: 'Not for dishonest gain' warns the shepherd against:
options: Using the flock as a means to his own profit or comfort
mc.why: The danger is making the flock a means to personal gain — money, comfort, or status.

mc.stem: 'Nor as being lords over those entrusted to you, but being examples' teaches that the leader should:
options: Drive the sheep with a heavy hand
Lead from the front as an example
mc.why: Christ leads by going first; the shepherd says 'Follow me as I follow Christ,' not 'Obey from afar.'

mc.stem: In the ancient world, a steward was someone who:
options: Managed a house that belonged to his master
Was a slave with no duties
mc.why: A steward ran the master's house, holding the keys but owning nothing, and would give account.

mc.stem: According to Hebrews 13:17, leaders watch primarily over the people's:
mc.why: Hebrews says they 'watch for your souls, as those who must give account' — souls come first.

mc.stem: Why must leaders watch so carefully, according to Hebrews 13:17?
options: Because they must give account to God
mc.why: They watch as those who must give account to God for the souls entrusted to them.

mc.stem: The steward image turns church administration into:
options: A sacred trust managed for the Master
mc.why: Every roster and meeting is the managing of a house that belongs to Another, a sacred trust.

mc.stem: What reward does 1 Peter 5:4 promise the faithful undershepherd?
options: A crown of glory that does not fade away
mc.why: When the Chief Shepherd appears, the faithful shepherd receives an unfading crown of glory.

mc.stem: The Chief Shepherd whom the undershepherd serves is best described as:
options: The One who laid down His life for the sheep
mc.why: He is not a hard master but the One who gave His life for the sheep and rewards His shepherds.

mc.stem: When a leader begins to think of the church as 'his own,' the unit warns he becomes:
mc.why: Forgetting the flock is God's and treating it as his own is a slow, respectable form of theft.

mc.stem: The shepherd leads the sheep by:
options: Going ahead so they follow his voice
Leaving them to find their own way
Driving them from behind like cattle
mc.why: A shepherd goes before the sheep and they follow his voice; he does not drive them like cattle.

mc.stem: In the illustration, why did people stay with the second pastor?
options: He led from among them and set the example
He never asked anything of them
mc.why: Both preached the same doctrine; the second led by example rather than lording over the flock.

mc.stem: The wolves a shepherd protects the flock from include:
options: False teaching, division, discouragement, and sin
mc.why: The dangers are false teaching, division, and the slow predators of discouragement and sin.

mc.stem: Earthly crowns leaders chase (bigger church, name, applause) are described as:
mc.why: Earthly crowns fade, often within a man's own lifetime; only the Chief Shepherd's crown never fades.

mc.stem: Because his reward is the Master's approval, the undershepherd can:
options: Pour himself out without bitterness and lead without grasping
mc.why: Seeking the Master's 'Well done,' not the flock's praise, frees him to serve without bitterness or grasping.

mc.stem: The central claim of Unit 2 is that the pastor is fundamentally:
options: The owner and master of the church
An undershepherd and steward accountable to the Chief Shepherd
mc.why: Unit 2 defines the leader as undershepherd and steward, accountable to the Chief Shepherd.

sa.prompt: Explain what it means that the pastor is an 'undershepherd,' and why the word 'under' matters.
sa.model: To be an undershepherd means the pastor is a real shepherd with real authority, but he serves under the Chief Shepherd, Jesus Christ. The word 'under' matters because the flock is the flock of God, bought by Christ and belonging to Him, not to the pastor. He does not own the sheep; he serves them on behalf of their true owner and will give account to Him. The moment a leader forgets that small word and treats the church as his own, he stops shepherding and begins, slowly, to steal what belongs to Christ.

sa.prompt: Name and briefly explain the shepherd's three basic tasks.
sa.model: The shepherd's three tasks are to feed, to lead, and to protect. He feeds the flock by bringing them to the pasture of God's Word, taught plainly enough that ordinary believers can eat and grow. He leads them by going ahead so they follow his voice, rather than driving them from behind like cattle. And he protects them by standing between the flock and danger — false teaching, division, discouragement, and sin, the wolves that would scatter or devour them. A leader who only feeds becomes a lecturer; one who only leads becomes a driver; the true shepherd does all three because the sheep need all three.

sa.prompt: 1 Peter 5:2-3 gives three contrasts about HOW to shepherd. Explain them.
sa.model: Peter gives three contrasts that search the shepherd's heart and motive. First, not by compulsion but willingly: the man who serves only because he feels trapped has the wrong heart, for God loves a willing shepherd. Second, not for dishonest gain but eagerly: the man who shepherds for money, comfort, or status has made the flock a means to his own ends. Third, not lording it over the flock but being an example: the man who drives the sheep with a tyrant's heavy hand has forgotten that Christ leads by going first. The true shepherd leads from the front and says, 'Follow me as I follow Christ.'

sa.prompt: What is a steward, and how does the steward image apply to a church leader?
sa.model: A steward is one who manages a great house that is not his own. He holds the keys, runs the affairs, and commands the servants, but everything he touches belongs to his master, and one day the master will call him to settle accounts. Applied to a church leader, this means he manages the Lord's house as a trust, owning nothing of it himself. Every roster, meeting, and decision is the handling of what belongs to Another, and he will give account to God. This turns administration from a worldly chore into a sacred trust, so the faithful steward handles even the smallest matter with care.

sa.prompt: According to Hebrews 13:17, what do leaders watch over, and why so carefully?
sa.model: Hebrews 13:17 says leaders watch for the people's souls, as those who must give account. What they watch is not first the budget or the building but souls — the eternal wellbeing of the people. And they watch so carefully because they must give account for those souls to God Himself. This accountability is what makes the work a sacred trust rather than a job: the leader handles the Lord's people knowing that the Master will one day ask how he cared for what was His, and nothing entrusted to him is too small to answer for.

sa.prompt: Contrast lording over the flock with leading by example, using the illustration of the two pastors.
sa.model: The first pastor lorded over his people, ruling like a foreman: every decision and every credit his, every dissenter pushed out. His church was orderly but cold and slowly emptied. The second pastor led by example from among his people, first to arrive and last to leave, first to apologize, doing himself what he asked of others. Both preached the same doctrine, but one drove the sheep and the other drew them. People follow a leader who drives them only as far as they must, but they follow a leader who draws them by example to the ends of the earth. This is Peter's point: lead from the front, not with a heavy hand.

sa.prompt: What reward does the Chief Shepherd promise, and how does it change the way a leader serves?
sa.model: First Peter 5:4 promises that when the Chief Shepherd appears, the faithful shepherd will receive a crown of glory that does not fade away. This changes everything about how a leader serves. The earthly crowns men chase — a bigger church, a greater name, applause — all fade, often within a lifetime, but the Chief Shepherd's crown never fades. Because his true reward is the Master's 'Well done,' not the flock's praise, the undershepherd can pour himself out without bitterness and lead without grasping. He serves a Master who gave His own life for the sheep and who is coming back to reward His faithful shepherds.

sa.prompt: Why is feeding the flock essential, and what is the 'pasture' for the church?
sa.model: Feeding the flock is essential because sheep cannot feed themselves; they must be led to good pasture or they starve and weaken. For the church, that pasture is the Word of God. The shepherd's task is to bring the people to Scripture and teach it plainly enough that ordinary believers, not only scholars, can eat and grow. A flock that is never fed will not mature no matter how well it is organized, because growth comes from the Word. So the leader who would shepherd well makes the faithful teaching of Scripture central, ensuring the sheep are nourished and built up in the faith.

sa.prompt: How does remembering 'I must give account' shape the way a leader handles small, practical matters?
sa.model: Remembering that he must give account makes a leader handle even small, practical matters with care, because he knows nothing in the Lord's house is too small to answer for. The steward manages a house that belongs to his Master, and the Master is coming home to settle accounts; so the roster, the meeting, the repair, and the hard conversation are all part of a sacred trust, not beneath him. A leader who forgets the account grows careless with 'minor' things; the one who remembers it is faithful in little as well as much, treating each detail as the managing of what belongs to God.

sa.prompt: Summarize Unit 2: what two pictures define the church leader, and what do they together teach?
sa.model: Unit 2 defines the church leader by two pictures: the undershepherd and the steward. As undershepherd, he feeds, leads, and protects a flock that is not his own but God's, serving willingly and eagerly, leading by example rather than lording it over the people, under the Chief Shepherd. As steward, he manages the Lord's house and watches for souls as one who must give account to God. Together they teach that the leader owns nothing and answers for everything: the church belongs to Christ, the leader serves and accounts for it, and his reward is the unfading crown the Chief Shepherd gives to those who shepherd His flock faithfully.
